claim: Litter decomposition is a key process determining elemental cycling in terrestrial ecosystems.
source: Litter decomposition is a key process determining elemental cycling in terrestrial ecosystems (Schlesinger and Bernhardt, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schlesinger and Bernhardt, 2020

claim: Decomposition is controlled by climate, litter quality, and origin, and the identity and abundance of microbial and faunal decomposers.
source: Decomposition is controlled by climate, litter quality, and origin, and the identity and abundance of microbial and faunal decomposers (Bradford et al., 2016; Joly et al., 2023; Swift et al., 1979).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bradford et al., 2016; Joly et al., 2023; Swift et al., 1979

claim: Climate regulates decomposition rates directly, but also indirectly by influencing food-web structure and dynamics.
source: Climate regulates decomposition rates directly, but also indirectly by influencing food-web structure and dynamics (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2021

claim: Theory suggests that decomposition is positively associated with moisture and temperature.
source: Theory suggests that decomposition is positively associated with moisture and temperature (Swift et al., 1979).
evidence: Supported by citation to Swift et al., 1979

claim: Plant litter decomposition in microbial litter bags is faster under warm and wet conditions than under cool and dry conditions.
source: Cross-site studies, reviews, and meta-analyses verified this global pattern, showing that plant litter decomposition in microbial litter bags is indeed faster under warm and wet conditions than under cool and dry conditions (Berg et al., 1993; Meentemeyer, 1978; Bradford et al., 2017; Parton et al., 2007; Aerts, 1997; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations: Berg et al., 1993; Meentemeyer, 1978; Bradford et al., 2017; Parton et al., 2007; Aerts, 1997; Zhang et al., 2008

claim: The prevailing understanding of decomposition implicitly assumes that microorganisms dominate plant litter decomposition, largely ignoring the role of animals.
source: This well accepted realization implicitly assumes that microorganisms dominate plant litter decomposition, largely ignoring the growing recognition that animals may play an important role in litter cycling.
evidence: Inference from the text about prevailing assumptions in the field

claim: Animals play an important role in litter cycling through mineralizing and excreting assimilated plant nutrients, fragmenting and partly decomposing plant material, and transporting detritus to microbial havens.
source: This role includes mineralizing and excreting assimilated plant nutrients, fragmenting and partly decomposing plant material, and transporting detritus to microbial havens (David, 2014; Frouz, 2018; Griffiths et al., 2021; Auclerc et al., 2022; Sagi et al., 2021; Coulis et al., 2016; Joly et al., 2018; Joly et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations: David, 2014; Frouz, 2018; Griffiths et al., 2021; Auclerc et al., 2022; Sagi et al., 2021; Coulis et al., 2016; Joly et al., 2018; Joly et al., 2020

claim: Faunal decomposition shows a positive association with temperature and precipitation.
source: Attempts to explore how climate affects faunal decomposition revealed a similar positive association with temperature and precipitation (García-Palacios et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to García-Palacios et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2020

claim: Soil animals of various size groups respond differently to climate.
source: This global pattern, however, may be confounded by compiling the effect of all decomposer fauna together, ignoring the well-established understanding that soil animals of various size groups respond differently to climate (Swift et al., 1979; Johnston and Sibly, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Swift et al., 1979; Johnston and Sibly, 2020

claim: Larger arthropods can survive and remain active during hot and dry periods when smaller organisms cannot.
source: Specifically, larger arthropods can survive and remain active during hot and dry periods when smaller organisms cannot (Cloudsley-Thompson, 1975).

claim: Macro-detritivorous arthropods dominate litter and wood decomposition in warm drylands, especially during warm and dry seasons.
source: Indeed, handful of evidence shows that macro-detritivorous arthropods dominate litter and wood decomposition in warm drylands, especially during warm and dry seasons (Veldhuis et al., 2017; Sagi et al., 2019; Zanne et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Veldhuis et al., 2017; Sagi et al., 2019; Zanne et al., 2022

claim: Detritivorous animals are expected to be exceptionally abundant in arid ecosystems where plant detritus is prevalent year-round but green plant material is available predominantly in short pulses following precipitation events.
source: Detritivorous animals are expected to be exceptionally abundant in arid ecosystems where plant detritus is prevalent year-round but green plant material is available predominantly in short pulses following precipitation events (Ayal et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ayal et al., 2005

claim: Macrofauna are physiologically and morphologically more adapted to aridity than mesofauna.
source: Macrofauna are physiologically and morphologically more adapted to aridity than mesofauna (Cloudsley-Thompson, 1975).

claim: The large size of macrofauna enables them to remain active during long dry periods by shuttling between existing and self-engineered climatic havens and the hostile foraging grounds on the surface.
source: Moreover, their large size enables them to remain active during long dry periods by shuttling between existing and self-engineered climatic havens and the hostile foraging grounds on the surface (Sagi and Hawlena, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sagi and Hawlena, 2021

claim: Macro-decomposition should be especially important in hot moisture-deprived habitats and periods, whereas the activity of microbes and mesofauna is expected to be minimal.
source: Consequently, macro-decomposition should be especially important in hot moisture-deprived habitats and periods, whereas the activity of microbes and mesofauna is expected to be minimal.
evidence: Logical inference from the previous statements about macrofauna adaptations

claim: In hyper-arid environments, extreme climatic conditions and scarce and unpredictable plant litter availability may limit macro-decomposer populations, diminishing macro-decomposition rates with increasing aridity.
source: In these environments, the extreme climatic conditions and scarce and unpredictable plant litter availability may limit macro-decomposer populations, diminishing macro-decomposition rates with increasing aridity.

claim: Macro-decomposition should follow a hump-shaped response to precipitation that peaks in arid ecosystems.
source: Consequently, and in sharp contrast to smaller organisms, macro-decomposition should follow a hump-shaped response to precipitation that peaks in arid ecosystems (Figure 1).
evidence: Hypothesis presented in text and illustrated in Figure 1

claim: The study examined plant litter decomposition by microorganisms, meso-decomposers, and macro-decomposers along an aridity gradient spanning from mean annual precipitation of 22–526 mm.
source: To test this novel hypothesis, we examined the climate dependency of plant litter decomposition by microorganisms, meso-decomposers, and macro-decomposers along a sharp aridity gradient spanning from mean annual precipitation (MAP) of 22–526 mm.

claim: The aridity gradient represents hyper-arid, arid, semiarid, and dry sub-humid Mediterranean climates.
source: This gradient represents hyper-arid, arid, semiarid, and dry sub-humid Mediterranean climates (Table 1, Figure 2A).
evidence: Description of study sites with reference to Table 1 and Figure 2A

claim: The experiment was repeated during hot summer with no precipitation and again during cooler and wetter winter.
source: We repeated the experiment during hot summer with no precipitation and again during cooler and wetter winter.

claim: Both microbial and mesofaunal decomposition should increase with increasing precipitation during the winter.
source: We hypothesized that both microbial and mesofaunal decomposition should increase with increasing precipitation during the winter, but during the dry summer contribute only minimally to plant litter decomposition across the aridity gradient.

claim: During the dry summer, microbial and mesofaunal decomposition should contribute only minimally to plant litter decomposition across the aridity gradient.
source: We hypothesized that both microbial and mesofaunal decomposition should increase with increasing precipitation during the winter, but during the dry summer contribute only minimally to plant litter decomposition across the aridity gradient.

claim: In the dry summer, macrofaunal decomposition should follow a hump-shaped response to precipitation, increasing from hyper-arid to arid sites and decreasing gradually in more mesic semiarid and Mediterranean sites.
source: In the dry summer, macrofaunal decomposition should follow a hump-shaped response to precipitation, increasing from hyper-arid to arid sites and decreasing gradually in more mesic semiarid and Mediterranean sites.

claim: The opposing climatic dependencies of macrofauna and microorganisms and mesofauna should lead to similar overall decomposition rates across the precipitation gradient except in the hyper-arid sites.
source: We also predicted that the opposing climatic dependencies of macrofauna and microorganisms and mesofauna should lead to similar overall decomposition rates across the precipitation gradient except in the hyper-arid sites in which decomposers activity is predicted to be minimal regardless of organism size (Figure 1).
evidence: Hypothesis stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1

claim: Hump-shaped relationships between precipitation and the abundance, richness, and biomass of macro-decomposers should peak in arid ecosystems.
source: We predicted hump-shaped relationships between precipitation and the abundance, richness, and biomass of macro-decomposers that peak in arid ecosystems.

claim: The litter removal rate was 1.3-fold higher in macro- than in meso-baskets on average.

claim: Litter removal was highest in the arid sites during summer and in the more mesic sites during winter.

claim: The semiarid Havat Shikmim site exhibited only a mesofaunal effect during both seasons.

evidence: Results from the experiment shown in Figure 3

claim: The macrofaunal, mesofaunal, and microorganismal contributions to litter mass loss peaked under arid, semiarid and Mediterranean climate conditions, respectively.
source: The macrofaunal, mesofaunal, and microorganismal contributions to litter mass loss peaked under arid, semiarid and Mediterranean climate conditions, respectively (Figure 4).

claim: Whole-community litter removal rates were comparable across the aridity gradient from Mediterranean to arid climate at the annual scale.

claim: The whole-community litter removal rate peaked in Sayeret Shaked (MAP = 148 mm).

claim: The whole-community litter removal rate significantly decreased under drier and wetter conditions than Sayeret Shaked.
source: In total, the whole-community litter removal rate peaked in Sayeret Shaked (MAP = 148 mm) and significantly decreased under drier and wetter conditions (Figure 4).

source: Meso- and macro-decomposition were similar in the hyper-arid and Mediterranean sites.

claim: Meso-decomposition was higher than macro-decomposition in the semiarid sites.
source: However, meso-decomposition was higher than macro-decomposition in the semiarid sites and much lower than macro-decomposition in the arid sites.

claim: Meso-decomposition was much lower than macro-decomposition in the arid sites.
source: However, meso-decomposition was higher than macro-decomposition in the semiarid sites and much lower than macro-decomposition in the arid sites.

claim: Meso-decomposers, like macro-decomposers, have adaptations that allow them to strive in moisture-deprived environments.
source: These results suggest that meso-decomposers, like macro-decomposers, have adaptations that allow them to strive in moisture-deprived environments.

claim: Meso-decomposition peaked in more mesic conditions than macro-decomposition, implying higher moisture dependency.
source: Yet, meso-decomposition peaked in more mesic conditions than macro-decomposition, implying higher moisture dependency.

claim: Faunal decomposition in this study peaked in arid environments, contrasting the positive association between faunal decomposition and precipitation found in recent global meta-analyses.
source: Faunal decomposition in our study peaked in arid environments, contrasting the positive association between faunal decomposition and precipitation that was found in recent global meta-analyses (García-Palacios et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: Comparison of study results with previous meta-analyses

claim: Previous studies may have underestimated faunal decomposition rates in drylands by grouping cold and dry environments together or focusing solely on precipitation without accounting for differences in temperature.
source: This discrepancy may reflect underestimation of faunal decomposition rates in drylands, possibly because these studies either deliberately grouped cold and dry environments together (García-Palacios et al., 2013; Wall et al., 2008), or focused solely on precipitation without accounting for differences in temperature (Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: Interpretation with citations to García-Palacios et al., 2013; Wall et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2020

claim: In cold water-deprived environments and seasons, low temperatures may limit the populations and activity of ectotherm animals.
source: In cold water-deprived environments and seasons, low temperatures may limit the populations and activity of ectotherm animals (Swift et al., 1979; Johnston and Sibly, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Swift et al., 1979; Johnston and Sibly, 2020

claim: The study used litter of one plant species (Stipa capensis) that is common to all seven experimental sites.
source: We used litter of one plant species that is common to all seven experimental sites.

claim: Using litter common to all sites allowed comparison of decomposition rates across sites without using exogenous litter.
source: In this way, we were able to compare decomposition rates across sites without using litter that is exogenous to one or more sites.

claim: Decomposer communities are assumed to perceive litter quality based on the chemical composition of the focal litter and past resource inputs.
source: Decomposer communities are assumed to perceive litter quality based on the chemical composition of the focal litter, and that of past resource inputs that these communities have experienced (Strickland et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Strickland et al., 2009

claim: Plant communities differ substantially between the study sites.
source: Plant communities differ substantially between our sites, suggesting that each decomposer community has experienced very different resource inputs, and may have access to alternative litter of various qualities.

claim: The perceived quality of S. capensis litter likely differs between sites.
source: Thus, it is likely that the perceived quality of S. capensis litter differs between sites, possibly confounding our results.

claim: The study sites were distributed along a single precipitation gradient.
source: Moreover, our sites were distributed along a single precipitation gradient.

claim: The results may be confounded by other environmental factors that were not accounted for.
source: Thus, our results may be confounded by other environmental factors that were not accounted for.

claim: Decomposers of varying size categories have different moisture dependencies.
source: In conclusion, our work revealed that decomposers of varying size categories have different moisture dependencies.

claim: Microorganisms, meso-decomposers, and macro-decomposers should be considered separately in decomposition models.
source: This suggests that microorganisms, meso-decomposers, and macro-decomposers should be considered separately in decomposition models, and emphasizes the need to contemplate animals' physiology and behavior when investigating zoogeochemical processes.

claim: Warm drylands cover 19% of the land surface worldwide and expand rapidly due to unsustainable land-use and climate change.
source: Warm drylands cover 19% of the land surface worldwide and expand rapidly due to unsustainable land-use and climate change (Cartereau et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cartereau et al., 2022

claim: Macro-decomposition in arid-lands compensates for the minimal microbial decomposition.
source: We highlight the importance of macro-decomposition in arid-lands that compensates for the minimal microbial decomposition, providing a plausible resolution to the long-debated dryland decomposition conundrum.

claim: The general conceptualization of decomposition is largely based on ample research from temperate ecosystems.
source: To date, the general conceptualization of decomposition is largely based on ample research from temperate ecosystems.
evidence: Statement about the state of the field

claim: Prevailing decomposition theory centers on focal processes that dominate decomposition in temperate systems.
source: Thus, prevailing theory centers on focal processes that dominate decomposition in these systems.
evidence: Inference about the state of the field

claim: In less studied ecosystems, additional processes like the role of animal decomposers may be dominant.
source: Our work highlights that in other less studied ecosystems additional processes like the role of animal decomposers may be dominant, opening the door for new exciting research that may shake our conceptualization of decomposition processes.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental findings and implications

claim: The study performed a manipulative litter mass loss experiment across seven sites representing a sharp MAP gradient ranging from hyper-arid desert to Mediterranean maquis.
source: We performed a manipulative litter mass loss experiment across seven sites representing a sharp MAP gradient ranging from hyper-arid desert to Mediterranean maquis (Figure 2A, Table 1).
evidence: Description of experimental design with reference to Figure 2A and Table 1

claim: All study sites were chosen to be on calcareous soils formed upon sedimentary limestone rock in natural habitats.
source: All sites were chosen to be on calcareous soils formed upon sedimentary limestone rock in natural habitats.

claim: The mean annual temperature varies only slightly across sites from 18.7 to 22.3°C.
source: The mean annual temperature varies only slightly across sites from 18.7 to 22.3°C.

claim: Micro-baskets allow entry of only microorganisms (<200 μm).
source: In each of the seven sites we installed litter baskets of three different mesh sizes that control organismal access to litter: micro-baskets allowing entry of only microorganisms (<200 μm), meso-baskets allowing entry of microorganisms and mesofauna (<2 mm), and macro-baskets that were identical to the meso-baskets but with side openings that allow entry of macrofauna (<2 cm).

claim: Meso-baskets allow entry of microorganisms and mesofauna (<2 mm).
source: In each of the seven sites we installed litter baskets of three different mesh sizes that control organismal access to litter: micro-baskets allowing entry of only microorganisms (<200 μm), meso-baskets allowing entry of microorganisms and mesofauna (<2 mm), and macro-baskets that were identical to the meso-baskets but with side openings that allow entry of macrofauna (<2 cm).

claim: Macro-baskets allow entry of macrofauna (<2 cm).
source: In each of the seven sites we installed litter baskets of three different mesh sizes that control organismal access to litter: micro-baskets allowing entry of only microorganisms (<200 μm), meso-baskets allowing entry of microorganisms and mesofauna (<2 mm), and macro-baskets that were identical to the meso-baskets but with side openings that allow entry of macrofauna (<2 cm).

claim: Litter baskets were filled with leaf litter belonging to the annual grass Stipa capensis Thunb. that is native to all seven study sites.
source: Litter baskets were filled with leaf litter belonging to the annual grass Stipa capensis Thunb. that is native to all seven study sites.

claim: Twenty-five blocks, each including the three basket types, were installed in each site for two consecutive experimental periods.
source: Twenty-five blocks, each including the three basket types (Figure 2B), were installed in each site for two consecutive experimental periods – a wet cool winter and a dry hot summer (2 periods × 7 sites × 3 treatments × 25 blocks = 1050 baskets in total).
evidence: Description of experimental design with reference to Figure 2B

claim: A total of 1050 baskets were used in the experiment.
source: Twenty-five blocks, each including the three basket types (Figure 2B), were installed in each site for two consecutive experimental periods – a wet cool winter and a dry hot summer (2 periods × 7 sites × 3 treatments × 25 blocks = 1050 baskets in total).

claim: The study characterized the macro-decomposer assemblage in each site during the two seasons using pitfall trapping.
source: We also characterized the macro-decomposer assemblage in each site during the two seasons using pitfall trapping.

claim: S. capensis litter was collected from the Avdat site in the summer of 2020 and air dried.
source: We collected S. capensis litter from the Avdat site in the summer of 2020 and air dried it.

claim: 3 ± 0.0001 g of litter was assigned to each litter basket.
source: We sorted the litter to remove litter belonging to any other species and assigned 3 ± 0.0001 g (Mettler Toledo MS105DU) to each litter basket.

claim: The litter baskets were 14 × 13 × 3.6 cm in size.
source: The 14 × 13 × 3.6 cm litter baskets were prepared of a 12-mm mesh galvanized welded metal, lined at the bottom with a 1.5-mm fiberglass mesh to prevent litter loss, and covered from all sides (including top and bottom) with a 2-mm metal mesh to exclude termites.

claim: In the macro-baskets, three 2 × 2 cm windows were cut at each of the four sides.
source: In the macro-baskets, three 2 × 2 cm windows were cut at each of the four sides.

claim: The windows in macro-baskets were cut approximately 1 cm above ground level to allow macrofaunal access but prevent accidental litter spill.
source: The windows were cut approximately 1 cm above ground level to allow macrofaunal access but prevent accidental litter spill.

claim: The window design may slightly reduce macrofaunal access, making estimations of the macrofaunal effect conservative.
source: This may slightly reduce macrofaunal access, making our estimations of the macrofaunal effect conservative.

claim: In the micro-baskets, the litter was placed within a polyethylene 200-μm mesh bag.
source: In the micro-baskets, we placed the litter within a polyethylene 200-μm mesh bag.

claim: The first batch of 525 litter baskets was installed in the field in November–December 2020.
source: We installed the first batch of 525 litter baskets in the field in November–December 2020.

claim: All blocks were placed around similarly sized bushes of locally distributed species and tethered to the ground using metal stakes.
source: All blocks were placed around similarly sized bushes of locally distributed species and tethered to the ground using metal stakes.

claim: The first batch of baskets was collected in May–July 2021.
source: We collected the baskets in May–July 2021 and replaced them with a new similar batch that was later collected in October–November 2021.

claim: The second batch of baskets was collected in October–November 2021.
source: We collected the baskets in May–July 2021 and replaced them with a new similar batch that was later collected in October–November 2021.

claim: An ash correction procedure was applied to account for dust accumulation on the litter.
source: To account for dust accumulation on the litter we applied an ash correction procedure (Barney et al., 2015).
evidence: Description of data processing method with citation to Barney et al., 2015

claim: Twenty pitfall traps were set up for 5–7 days at each site during each experimental period.
source: We characterized the macro-decomposer assemblages by setting up 20 pitfall traps for 5–7 days at each site during each experimental period.

claim: Wet season traps were opened in February 2021.
source: Wet season traps were opened in February 2021, whereas the dry season traps were opened between late August and early October.

claim: Dry season traps were opened between late August and early October.
source: Wet season traps were opened in February 2021, whereas the dry season traps were opened between late August and early October.

claim: Pitfall traps comprised 40% absolute ethanol, 40% distilled water, and 20% propylene glycol as preservative.
source: We added to each trap 150 ml of preservative, which comprised of 40% absolute ethanol, 40% distilled water, and 20% propylene glycol.

claim: Only animals larger than 2 mm were included in the pitfall trap analysis.
source: Samples were sorted and identified to morphospecies level in the lab. Only animals larger than 2 mm were included in the analysis.

claim: The random effect of the experimental spatial blocks was found insignificant using a simulation test with 9999 simulations (RLRT = 2.1, p-value = 0.07).
source: The random effect of the experimental spatial blocks was found insignificant using a simulation test with 9999 simulations (RLRT = 2.1, p-value = 0.07).

claim: Microbial contribution to litter mass loss was defined as the mass loss from micro-baskets.
source: Microbial contribution was defined as the mass loss from micro-baskets; mesofaunal contribution was calculated as the difference between mass loss from meso- and micro-baskets; macrofaunal contribution was calculated as the difference between mass loss from macro- and meso-baskets; whole-community decomposition was defined as the mass loss from macro-baskets.

claim: Mesofaunal contribution to litter mass loss was calculated as the difference between mass loss from meso- and micro-baskets.
source: Microbial contribution was defined as the mass loss from micro-baskets; mesofaunal contribution was calculated as the difference between mass loss from meso- and micro-baskets; macrofaunal contribution was calculated as the difference between mass loss from macro- and meso-baskets; whole-community decomposition was defined as the mass loss from macro-baskets.

claim: Macrofaunal contribution to litter mass loss was calculated as the difference between mass loss from macro- and meso-baskets.
source: Microbial contribution was defined as the mass loss from micro-baskets; mesofaunal contribution was calculated as the difference between mass loss from meso- and micro-baskets; macrofaunal contribution was calculated as the difference between mass loss from macro- and meso-baskets; whole-community decomposition was defined as the mass loss from macro-baskets.

claim: Whole-community decomposition was defined as the mass loss from macro-baskets.
source: Microbial contribution was defined as the mass loss from micro-baskets; mesofaunal contribution was calculated as the difference between mass loss from meso- and micro-baskets; macrofaunal contribution was calculated as the difference between mass loss from macro- and meso-baskets; whole-community decomposition was defined as the mass loss from macro-baskets.

claim: The relationship between MAP and decomposition contributions was modeled using Locally Estimated Scatterplot Smoothing.
source: We modeled the relationship between MAP and each of these contributions using Locally Estimated Scatterplot Smoothing.

claim: Differences in the macro-decomposer assemblage among experimental sites and seasons were assessed using a principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) with Bray-Curtis index as the dissimilarity metric.
source: We assessed differences in the macro-decomposer assemblage among experimental sites and seasons using a principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) with individual traps as the sampling units and BC index as the dissimilarity metric.

claim: Differences across sites and seasons in macro-decomposer assemblage were tested using a permutational multivariate analysis of variance.
source: We tested for differences across sites and seasons in macro-decomposer assemblage using a permutational multivariate analysis of variance, followed by pairwise comparisons between sites using the Benjamini–Hochberg p-value adjustment.
